speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House of Commons of Canada has suffered another conspicuous loss in the passing of one who for many years took a prominent part in its proceedings.
James Shaver Woodsworth, whose death occurred on Saturday, was first returned to parliament as member for Winnipeg North Centre at the general elections of 1921. Mr. Woodsworth was returned at each subsequent general election. In all he was a member of the parliament of Canada for over twenty years. He came to parliament first as a representative of labour, and continued as a member of a small labour group until the formation, in 1932, of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. He was one of the founders of the federation, and became its president, and also its leader in the House of Commons.
Immediately following the general elections of 1940, Mr. Woodsworth suffered a serious impairment of health from which he never recovered. Though he made an appearance in this chamber in November of last year, it was only for a day or two. His health was such that he was unable to take any part in its proceedings.
In these years, when momentous changes are taking place in all parts of the world, and unprecedented events follow each other with unparalleled rapidity, the past tends to become quickly obliterated. New names, new issues, new situations, for the time being at least, obscure the old. Few names associated with the public life of Canada could better illustrate this truth than that of the late member for Winnipeg North Centre.
Mr. Woodsworth took no part in the proceedings of this House of Commons which was elected in the spring of 1940. Many present day members of the house would have difficulty in realizing that during the preceding twenty years there were few voices oftener

heard in debate than his. There were, indeed, few opponents of the administration, regardless of its political complexion, who were more frequent, and at times more scathing, in their criticisms. One had to know Mr. Woodsworth personally and to be acquainted with the background of his political life, to appreciate him at his true worth. He was, when speaking in public, so constant in his criticisms, so downright in his denunciations, that it was difficult to realize how genuinely kindly, simple and sympathetic his real nature was. Not a few were all too readily inclined to describe him as a demagogue. To my mind, of men who have occupied seats in our parliament and have risen to position of leadership, Mr. Woodsworth was one of the most sincere and least self-seeking.
The truth is that Mr. Woodsworth remained to the end what he was from the outset, the missionary of a great cause. That cause was the well-being of his fellowmen. Social reform was the interest which lay nearest to his heart. To this interest, as a young man, he gave expression in different ways. He began his life work as a member of the Christian ministry. In this calling, he had succeeded his father who had been a Methodist minister. He prepared himself for the ministry by a course in arts at the university of Manitoba, and later by a course in theology at Victoria college, university of Toronto, and by post-graduate studies at Oxford. The knowledge thus acquired was subsequently supplemented by firsthand contacts with industrial conditions in England and Canada and by social research. Before and during his years in parliament, as preacher and teacher and writer, he sought to awaken the conscience of his fellow men to social injustices. In these injustices, he believed, lay the seeds of discontent and widespread disorder. Equally he strove, by advocating a wider tolerance and better understanding, to remove barriers of race and class and creed, and to establish more in the way of economic freedom and social equality.
In parliament, this spirit also manifested itself in the continuous advocacy and support of many measures of social reform. He be-leived in service as the highest of human motives, and exemplified his belief by his own untiring efforts on behalf of the cause he had so much at heart. He had come to feel that the widest opportunity for service and for the enjoyment of the fruits of service could be secured to the masses of men only by a radical change in the existing order of society. This led to an advocacy of socialistic measures and policies which made him a storm centre of some of the political controversy of the recent past. This controversy, as I have

James S. Woodsworth
already suggested, served to obscure, and, I believe at times, to thwart his ,real purpose.
To nothing was Mr. Woodsworth more passionately opposed than to any form of militarism. He was an out-and-out pacifist. Regardless of the antagonism toward himself, which this attitude served to arouse, and the sacrifices it entailed, he held to it to the last.
Philosophically, he was doubtless right in the belief that, in the end, force accomplishes nothing positive; that it is a mistaken method of achieving enduring results. What he failed to see was that, while, in the long run, reason alone can hold the true supremacy, reason must be afforded the opportunity to prevail. All chance to apply reason to the solution of human problems may be forever lost if those who seek to conquer by the sword are not made to perish by the sword. I shall always believe that it was the mental conflict between the idealism of Mr. Woodsworth's hopes and beliefs, and the realism of the horrors of nazism and fascism, that crushed his spirit and broke his strength.
It is too soon to judge the place that Mr. Woodsworth's name will come to hold in the annals of this parliament and in the history of our country. I, for one, believe it will have a high and honoured place, not because of the political doctrines he espoused, and with which a part of his public life was so closely identified-though, even here, it may yet come to be said of him as of other social reformers, that he was ahead of his times-but because of his upright character and his fearless advocacy of the right as it was given him to see the right. His independence of thought and personal integrity, his sterling qualities of honesty and industry, his courageous championship of the causes to which, by conviction, he was wedded, won for him the admiration even of those to whom he was politically opposed.
Mr. Woodsworth has left a name which is greatly respected in our parliament and country. It will, I believe, be increasingly honoured with the passing of the years.
I should like to extend to my hon. friend the member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), the present leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, and to the members of his party the very sincere sympathy of all hon. members on this side of the house, and particularly may I express a word of sympathy on behalf of us all to the late member's son-in-law, the member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), and to Mrs. Maclnnis. I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, on behalf of all members of the House of Commons, to convey
our sincere and deep sympathy to Mrs. Woodsworth and to the other members of her family in their great bereavement.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: JAMES S. WOODSWORTH   TRIBUTE TO THE MEMORY OF THE LATE LEADER OF THE COOPERATIVE COMMONWEALTH FEDERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again the grim reaper has intervened' and taken his harvest from among our membership. Once again we are reminded of what fleeting figures we are on this stage of public life.
In the death of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, a figure which attracted attention from coast to coast for more than two decades has passed into the great beyond.
I well recall my first view of Mr. Woodsworth in the first session of the fourteenth parliament in 1922, when we both took our seats in the house for the first time.
A year or two previously, shortly after the Winnipeg strike, I had visited that city and had heard various tales of Mr. Woodsworth's activities at that time. I was curious to see him in the flesh. He had been painted to me as a socialist, almost a communist, as an agitator, and a demagogue. I was curious to know what his course of action would be in this house, having regard to what I had heard as well as to what I knew of his education, his background and his family traditions, having had, as he did, a pioneer Wesleyan minister for a father, and a mother of united empire loyalist stock.
I had not long to wait. This house met on March 8. The debate on the motion on the address in reply began on the thirteenth and on the following day Mr. Woodsworth entered the debate. If hon. members care to review the record they will find that in that first speech he dealt with a great variety of national problems, running through the whole gamut of economic disturbances, unemployment, unemployment insurance, production, the defence department and the problems of reconstruction. I then formed the opinion that here was a man who was intensely in earnest; a man who had strong opinions and the ability to express them. To some he may have appeared as a fanatic. However that may be, I think no one ever doubted' his sincerity and honesty of purpose.
Throughout the succeeding years, whether in the House of Commons or on the public platform, he pursued his 'purpose and supported his ideals. Down through those years he fought for the under-dog, for social amelioration and for social justice. And he lived long enough to witness the fruition of two of his cherished policies-old age pensions and unemployment insurance.
James S. Woodsworth

I like to think that in his later years he had mellowed and had softened1 his opinions. I recall our last conversation in November last. Although unable to take part in the business of the session he had come to Ottawa for a brief period, shattered in health and wearied with the struggle. I called upon him in his office, and we discussed many matters- the state of the nation, the war situation, his health, and the probability of his return to active participation in public life. I left him with a sincere feeling of respect. Here was a man who had gone through the fire of adversity, through a stormy public life, and who had emerged with a philosophy of life, unchanged in its objectives, but full of charity and with some understanding of the viewpoint of those from whom he had differed.
To his loved ones, to the members of his party in this house, particularly his son-in-law, the member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), I offer on behalf of myself and those associated with me our sincere expressions of sympathy in the loss they have sustained.

maintopic: JAMES S. WOODSWORTH   TRIBUTE TO THE MEMORY OF THE LATE LEADER OF THE COOPERATIVE COMMONWEALTH FEDERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after the eloquent tributes which have been paid to-day to Mr. Woodsworth by the leaders of the two main parties, there remains little indeed for me to say. I shall merely attempt a sketch of Mr. Woodsworth as he appealed to me in the several years during which I was here in his company in this parliament.
I was impressed at all times with the surprising energy of the man and the courage which prompted him to plunge into the most painful positions and fight his way through- an industry which never seemed to fail, and a hope and faith which were constantly in evidence. I was surprised at the persistence which characterized him even when it looked as though there was no chance of achieving his objective. His sincerity no one could possibly doubt. In readiness and skill as a debater he had I think very few equals, if any, in this house during the time I have been here.
Mr. Woodsworth's life recalls to me some lines of Browning which have always delighted me. Perhaps I may be pardoned if I quote them:
One who never turned his hack but marched breast forward,
Never doubted clouds would break,
Never dreamed, though right were worsted, wrong would triumph,
Held we fall to rise, are baffled to fight better,
Sleep to wake.

Mr. Woodsworth was many times baffled but always ?ose to fight better, and now that he has gone asleep I think it is the wish and the hope and the faith of everyone here that he will wake to take up the struggle for humanity in another sphere.
To Mrs. Woodsworth and his children I would commend the fine character of a husband and father whose life can be to them a matter of rejoicing and a constant example and inspiration. To the members of his party bereaved of their leader I also express the sincerest sympathy.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. T. THORSON (Minister of National War Services):
maintopic: JAMES S. WOODSWORTH   TRIBUTE TO THE MEMORY OF THE LATE LEADER OF THE COOPERATIVE COMMONWEALTH FEDERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I
desire to add my personal tribute to the memory of a great and courageous humanitarian.
Mrs. DORISE W. NIELSEN (North Battleford): Mr. Speaker, I should deem it an honour if you would allow me to express the feelings which I know are shared by so many Canadians.
A pioneer has passed on. In years gone by, when pioneers in new social thought were few, Mr. Woodsworth worked untiringly. Many were the old decayed trees of prejudice he felled, and much of the underbrush of fear and misunderstanding he cleared. He cultivated the minds of our people and planted the good seed.
In paying tribute, Mr. Speaker, to his memory I wish to convey to Mrs. Woodsworth the appreciation, we have of the part she has played. Long years of love and devotion she has given, not only to her husband but to the ideals and ideas which he laboured to promote. Many an hour of companionship in her husband's company she courageously sacrificed, and because of her help, sympathy and understanding Mr. Woodsworth was able to give so much of his time and thought to the problems of the common people. No tribute to Mr. Woodsworth would be complete without a recognition of the part his wife has also played.
Many a year yet he might have spent with his wife and family had he not given so unstintingly of his health and strength in the cause so dear to his heart.
It is my sincere wish that the regret and sorrow which they and we feel at his passing may be lightened by the sure knowledge that in the fullness of time his labours will bear fruit. When the full light of a new

James S. Woodsworth
society floods the world we shall remember the man who saw its first pale gleam and so consistently followed it.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources):
maintopic: JAMES S. WOODSWORTH   TRIBUTE TO THE MEMORY OF THE LATE LEADER OF THE COOPERATIVE COMMONWEALTH FEDERATION
speechtext:
It is now almost
thirty years, Mr. Speaker, since I first met the late Mr. Woodsworth. We were fellow townsmen of the city of Winnipeg. On the occasion on which I met him he was doing some work in connection with foreign settlements located in various parts of western Canada. I was impressed from the beginning by the earnestness of the man, the vision he possessed, and the thought he had as to how these newcomers to Canada should be assisted in becoming acquainted not only with Canadian institutions but with the whole picture of Canadian life.
I have followed his subsequent career with a great deal of interest. There were ocasions upon which I differed from him, but there was never for a moment any question in my mind of the sincerity, the integrity and the courage of the man. He was one who at all times had the courage of his convictions, and I am always ready to pay a tribute to a man possessed of these qualities of honesty, sincerity and courage. Men of this type are far too rare in the life of our country.
He has passed to the great beyond where, sooner or later, all must go, but he has left behind him a record of which his family may well be proud. He has rendered a service to this country, and, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has said, it may well be reported of him in the years to come that the policies he advocated were the forerunners of policies which yet may come to pass in this country.
I simply wish to join in this tribute of sincere admiration of his character, and to express my sympathy with all the members of his family.

maintopic: JAMES S. WOODSWORTH   TRIBUTE TO THE MEMORY OF THE LATE LEADER OF THE COOPERATIVE COMMONWEALTH FEDERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, parliament and the entire country mourn in the person of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, Mr. J. S. Woodsworth, a man of wide culture, an ardent patriot and a renowned orator. The eloquence of this great Canadian which stirred and charmed the members of this house over a period of almost twenty years, stemmed from deep conviction as well as from extraordinary dialectic powers. May I be permitted to offer to the bereaved members of his family and particularly to the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), my heartfelt sympathy.
May I also express my deep sympathy to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and the hon. members of whom he remains the distinguished leader.
(Text) Mr. Woodsworth was a man of honour and courage and a great Canadian; and the country will never forget him.

maintopic: JAMES S. WOODSWORTH   TRIBUTE TO THE MEMORY OF THE LATE LEADER OF THE COOPERATIVE COMMONWEALTH FEDERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, because I knew Mr. Woodsworth intimately since 1897, meeting him then at many athletic contests between rival colleges, and because we met together on many occasions and discussed ways and' means for the betterment of the underprivileged, I invited him often to our church, at a time when such invitations were not always popular. He never betrayed a trust; he always acted like a Christian gentleman. While we were both in Ottawa he often called me in and we discussed things together. I shall not soon forget my visits to him in the hospital. As I was leaving the first time he said, "Your visit is refreshing; come back again, and do not leave without a word a prayer." I appreciated his words.
To me James Woodsworth was a practical Christian, because I believe the Christian programme is: feed the hungiy, clothe the naked, visit the sick and go to those in prison. He practised those principles, and men are known by their conduct. He always struggled on behalf of the man who was underneath, and he did it without making anything out of it. I do not suppose he has left to his loved ones much of this world's goods; and believing that to be so, and having much in common with him, I would suggest to the government and to the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) that they consider seriously the provision of a pension for Mrs. Woodsworth.
I pay my tribute to him as a man of courage and conviction, one who was never afraid to champion the cause of the individual who was down.

maintopic: JAMES S. WOODSWORTH   TRIBUTE TO THE MEMORY OF THE LATE LEADER OF THE COOPERATIVE COMMONWEALTH FEDERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I, as the only
representative of the city of Winnipeg in the house at this moment, offer a short addition to the obituary references of those who have already spoken of J. S. Woodsworth.
His life for many years has been identified with my own city. Certain I am that I speak for all the people of that city in joining sincerely with others who have spoken to-day in

James S. Woodsworth
an expression of sympathy to the wife and family of this deceased member. From my acquaintance with, and experience of J. S. Woodsworth, I would say that the last thing he would ever desire would be any mournful thought about his departing or any sad references to it. Nor would he want me to speak of him any differently to-day from the way in which I customarily spoke of him when he was alive. I fancy that he went out happy to meet his Pilot face to face and secure in the belief that he was going to do so.
I knew J. S. Woodsworth longer than most members of parliament. There are only one or two in this house who have known 'him longer.
My first meeting with him was such that I have borne him in kindly remembrance ever since. Somewhere in the neighbourhood of 1909, when I was able to return to school studies after labouring at odd jobs for six or seven years, he was engaged in social service -and it was service-on behalf of the Methodist church. I went to him, a stranger, to get some information about a debate on immigration policies. I shall not soon forget the thoughtful kindness he exhibited in endeavouring to help me. Long after the event about which I had consulted him had gone by, he kept the problem in mind, and sent bits of information to me as these came to him from time to time. I consequently always remembered him as a man who was earnestly and guilelessly interested in other people.
It has already been well said -here to-day, and I -have heard it said thousands of times in Jim Wood-sworth's lifetime, that While one might sharply disagree with him, sharply disagree with his opinions, even to the point of being angry with him for holding and- expressing such opinions, one could not fail to respect the man himself, both because of his sincerity and because of his tenacity in holding to his view's.
Well, sir, we know that the wolf that is in the middle of the pack will soon be forgotten; it is the one on the edge of the -pack, or leading the pack that impresses itself on the mind. Woodsworth was never in the -middle of the pack.
Of all his attributes, I believe the principal one was his carelessness. Woodsworth was careless to an extent that would impel the majority of people to call him foolish. What I mean is that he was careless of what happened to him. He was unmindful of -himself. Wrong he may have been sometimes, but any wrongness was of the head; it was never of the heart. He was not engaged in trying to 
carve out of life something of material benefit for himself. In this respect Jim Woodsworth was egregious; he towered up out of the pack. Consequently I -predict that he will not soon -be forgotten. If there were more people in the -world, -more in Canada, yes, more in this parliament actuated by motives as free from desire for material gain as was Jim Woodsworth, the world and Canada, yes, and- this parliament itself, would -be better off; because the more individuals are actuated -by motives completely untinged with selfishness, the more likelihood -there is of their actions conducing to the real progress of mankind.
Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Seldom have we heard a finer tribute paid to one of our colleagues. I had known Mr. Woodsworth fairly well. He was in this house when I came in over seventeen years ago and he had always been very kind to me, as he was to any other colleague. He commanded universal respect not only in the city of Winnipeg where he lived, but throughout the country. He was always well informed on the problems that he discussed; particularly social matters, and as a debater he had a voice that carried very well. I shall remember him as a born gentleman, a gentleman of the old school, and those who had conversations with him will never forget the kindly glance in his eye when they spoke with him. He will be remembered for his integrity, his sincerity, his indomitable courage; and we shall all remember him as a great patriot who was Canadian at heart.
I join with the other speakers in conveying my deepest sympathy to Mrs. Woodsworth, to his children and to our esteemed colleague, the member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis).

maintopic: JAMES S. WOODSWORTH   TRIBUTE TO THE MEMORY OF THE LATE LEADER OF THE COOPERATIVE COMMONWEALTH FEDERATION
speechtext:
On behalf of the group which Mr. Woodsworth so ably led in this house, I desire to express to all who have spoken our deep appreciation of the kindly references that have been made to his life and to his work. I would say too that we appreciate all that has been said about his splendid helpmeet, Mrs. Woodsworth, who to-day is bereaved. Those of us who have known them through the years know that always in the background, standing sympathetically behind her husband, was the figure of a brave and good woman. And so we appreciate the kindly references that have been made to her.
For ourselves, we feel that we have lost a revered leader, a wise counsellor and a true friend. But as has already been said, his work

James S. Woodsivorth
will live and his influence will grow. I admired him for those sterling qualities which sprang from his pioneer background. He was a Canadian with roots deep in the soil of this country, and yet he was not narrow in any sense. A product of two of our Canadian universities; Manitoba and Toronto, and enjoying the additional advantage of having studied in the great university of Oxford, he brought to the problems of this country a very wide knowledge of social and economic conditions in many parts of the world!.
His work for the new Canadians will not be forgotten. They were always very dear to him, and often in our conferences he would tell us what fine qualities the Ukrainians had, the Ruthenians, the Doukhobors; how he knew and understood them, and hoped that one day they might be integrated into the structure of Canadian fellowship. The great test for him personally came perhaps in the first great war, when he gave up what might have been a life of comparative ease because of his conviction that war was wrong; that the conscription of men against their will was quite wrong. And so he stepped out of the calling which he had chosen as his life's work. He went out to the Pacific coast where for a time he did the hard labour of a longshoreman to earn his daily bread and maintain his young family. Those of us who knew him know what a torture it must have been to that frail body-for frail he was-to undergo the toil of unloading heavy freight from the ships plying between the Pacific coast and the orient.
He became a member of parliament in 1921. He was a great teacher. As a teacher myself I have heard him speaking with groups of young people; that was the thing he liked best to do. Between sessions, if we visited him in his home in Winnipeg we would always find groups of young people gathered in his study talking things over with him. And if I may betray a secret, he had hoped that he might retire before the last election and devote the remaining years of his life to teaching young Canadians how to be of greater service to their country. But that was not permitted to him; and to-day we mourn his loss.
I know it is generally recognized throughout this house that he was sincere. Sincerity and courage in his convictions were at the very root and base of his character. As the Prime Minister has said, quite truly, at times he was scathing in his criticisms in this house of what he considered to be wrong, scathing sometimes in reference to
people who occupied seats in this chamber; yet I have heard him on more than one occasion check those who in private conversation sought to belittle personally the present Prime Minister, the late leader of the opposition, and other hon. members of this house. He bore no personal animosity to anyone.
He had the characteristics of a prophet. I remember on one occasion I was on a platform with him and with Professor King Gordon, who had occupied the chair of Christian ethics at the Union theological college at McGill. We knew that some views that Mr. Woodsworth was expressing were unpopular with the audience. King Gordon leaned across to me and said, "There is only one person that I can remember of whom he reminds me, the ancient prophet Amos courageously denouncing the evils of the society of his day and generation." There was much of the scriptural prophet in J. S. Woodsworth.
His work will live. His influence will grow. The very name we bear, the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, was a suggestion of J. S. Woodsworth. He hoped that he might be permitted to help lay the foundations of a new order in Canada in which men and women would cooperate for the common good; hence the name. And that I think he did. I am quite sure that none who were here when this house decided that Canada should enter the war will ever forget the tensity of the scene. If I may say so, he always appreciated the kindly reference of the Prime Minister when, during the debate on participation in the war, just before Mr. Woodsworth rose to speak, the right hon. gentleman prepared the difficult path for him by saying that no matter what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre might say or do, this house would understand that he did it in all sincerity. That speech was his last major effort in parliament.
His last two years of life were beclouded by war-war against which he had fought so hard, war which he hoped might never come again; and when it came it did in reality crush him.
I think those of us who knew him can find no better epitaph for him than the words of Alexander Pope:
Statesman, yet friend to truth! of soul sincere,
In action faithful, and in honour clear;
Who broke no promise, served no private end,	.
Who gained no title, and who lost no friend.

subtopic: PRISONERS OF WAR
PRISONERS OF WAR
speechtext:
1.	Is the government satisfied that the duty of searching hospitals and prison camps for Canadian internees in enemy and enemy-occupied countries is being carried out efficiently, and have the next of kin of all officers and men been informed of the fate of their relatives, as far as possible?
2.	Are these searches being carried out by government agencies, or are they only undertaken by private organizations, and what are they?
3.	What status has the Red Cross in enemy countries, and where and how do they function from in Germany, Italy and Japan?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PRISONERS OF WAR
speechtext:
(As the situatiou with regard to information about Canadian prisoners of war and internees is most easily dealt with by separating the European and far eastern theatres of war, the answers are being given in two groups, the first referring to Germany and Italy including occupied territories and the second referring to Japan and Japanese occupied territories.)
Germany and Italy, including Occupied Territories:
1.	Information regarding Canadian prisoners of war and civilian internees is not obtained, strictly speaking, through the "searching" of hospitals and internment camps. According to the provisions of the Geneva Convention relating to the treatment of prisoners of war (1929), which is adhered to by the belligerents on both sides, belligerents are required to notify each other as soon as possible of all internees or prisoners through the intermediary of an information bureau set up by each detaining power for this purpose (article 8). The information bureau transmits all such information immediately to the powers concerned through the protecting power and through a special central agency set up by the International Red Cross committee at Geneva (article 77). As far as combatant prisoners of war are concerned, these provisions are observed by both 
sides, and lists of Canadian prisoners are telegraphed to both Ottawa and London as soon as this information is received at Geneva. The Department of National Defence notifies the next of kin after the information has been checked.
Information obtained in this way is supplemented by the representatives of the protecting power who are allowed to visit all internment camps housing Canadians, whether combatants or civilian internees, and lists furnished by the protecting power have so far been the chief source of information regarding civilians. The Geneva Convention has, however, been extended reciprocally to cover civilians as well as combatants, and official lists of civilian 'internees are now being provided.
2.	See answer to question No. 1.
3.	National Red Cross organizations as a rule deal exclusively with problems arising out of the care of their own nationals. This is understood to be the case in Germany and Italy. Activities connected with the whereabouts or welfare of Canadian prisoners of war and internees in these countries are handled by the International Red Cross and its official delegates, who are also authorized to visit any camp.
Japan and Japanese-Occupied Territories:
1.	Although Japan has not formally ratified the Geneva Convention, the Japanese government have stated that prisoners of war and internees will be treated in accordance with its provisions. A list of Canadian civilians interned in Japan has already been supplied both to the Argentine embassy at Tokyo and to the International Red Cross. Further lists of combatant prisoners are awaited.
2.	See answers to questions No. 1 and No. 3.
3.	With regard to the Japanese Red Cross, the situation is different from that in the other belligerent countries, in that it is understood that the Japanese Red Cross intends to take charge of some of the functions such as the distribution of parcels and comforts, which elsewhere are normally in the hands of the delegates of the International Red Cross.

Mr. Speaker, if the minister had used more diligence these resolutions would have been on the order paper a long time ago. There is just one limitation to that statement, and that is that one of the provinces had not entered into the final arrangements. I would like to point out to the minister that the time of the house in the debate on the address was taken up by nearly a hundred hon. members opposite, and the regular business of parliament was thus impeded for nearly a month. They took up three times as much time as hon. members on this side of the house, and their speeches on the plebiscite occupy three times as much space as that occupied by hon. members on this side. And yet the impression has gone out that we, and other hon. members on this side of the house, have sought to hold up government business. It is not true, and this occasion gives me the opportunity to say so.
The request which the minister now makes is quite reasonable. The legislatures are in session and they want to know the terms of the bills. To that I have no objection. But in withholding our objection in this instance we do not for one moment propose to give up our rights, nor do we propose that this procedure shall be taken by the government as a precedent for the violation of the rules of the house.
The minister has said there is no reason why we cannot debate the matter on the second reading of the bill. There is something in what he says, but it has been my experience that in the committee stage, by cross-examination and intelligent questioning, hon. members often bring out certain aspects of a public question which do not appear on the face of the motion. It is a valuable privilege accorded to members of parliament, and it is of value especially to those who are not promoting the legislation but are simply seeking information. It is a privilege which I say hon. members ought not to give up except in most exceptional cases.
I know the minister is anxious to have these bills introduced-and of course he does not propose to proceed with them until after the Easter vacation. We shall have ample time during the vacation to study the proposed legislation, and see what is in it. These agreements are most complicated. As opportunity has offered I have attempted to master



Income and Corporation Tax
some of them, and I can say that they are highly technical. They are full of legalities which will require the study of hon. members.
I cannot possibly study nine different agreements. I am trying to confine myself to one or two, and I would hope that hon. members on both sieves of the house, representing the various provinces, will take it upon themselves to get copies of these agreements and to study their effect upon their own provinces. After all we are not only citizens of Canada; we come from the various provinces, and I believe we should see how this matter affects our provinces.
I know the position with respect to New Brunswick, and it has not worked out according to plan. New Brunswick is giving up the income tax municipally-not provincially, because we have no provincial income tax. It is giving up corporation taxation, and the amount of taxes thus collected from us by the municipality is being transferred to the dominion treasury, and is being multiplied many times. I am not objecting to that, because this country is at war. But in New Brunswick we are being mulcted in new taxation to make up what is being transferred. I do not think anyone objects to the increase in rate of income tax we have to pay for federal war purposes. But I thought-and I think the country was led to believe-that the grants in aid made by the dominion to the provinces in lieu of the tax field vacated would be passed on in full to the municipalities. That, I believed, was the intention. What has happened? We are having new taxation in New Brunswick. It is taxation of a class or kind we never had before, taxation which under any name is additional taxation on real estate. And we will never be clear of it; I have made up my mind to that. After the field is vacated we shall have to pay the additional taxation, and I protest against that position.
So far as I am concerned I am quite agreeable to the minister doing what he wishes, subject to the reservations I have made.

The Minister of Munitions and Supply says that it is not his business to distribute these contracts on any other basis than efficiency of production, and I agree entirely with him. I have spoken on this subject before. I remember the question came up in the house about six or eight months after the fall of France. I was able to say at that time that I thought the work of the Department of Munitions and Supply had been a series of splendid or brilliant improvisations. That is just about what it was. The department was forced to get things quickly, and to do so, turned to the area of centralized industry. Unquestionably that was the right thing to do. From the point of view of a department which is interested chiefly in getting out guns, ships and all kinds of equipment, I believe the attitude taken by the Minister of Munitions and Supply is not to be criticized.
On the other hand I do say that governments mu$t consider the social consequences of the courses they may follow. There is certainly too great a concentration of works here in the east, in that portion recently described
by one writer as "the wedge." He was referring to the district bounded by Montreal, North Bay and Windsor. Perhaps it might be called a triangle.
Now I hold in my hand a letter received either to-day or yesterday from the Industrial Development Board of Manitoba. I submit it is a reasonable letter, and I should like to place it on record as substantially expressing my own views with reference to this problem. The letter addressed to me, states:
Thi3 hoard desires to direct your attention to the situation in Manitoba with respect to lack of war production, idle plants and idle men, many with industrial experience.
Relief rolls which had decreased to a very considerable extent during 1941 are now on the increase, for example the number of families on relief in Winnipeg was 535 at the end of last October and has now increased to 710 and is growing every day.
Perhaps I should interject that it is usual in February and part of March for relief rolls to increase. That has been my experience in my constituency. Nevertheless that is a very heavy increase at this juncture of our national life. The letter continues:
The Labour Gazette shows there were 8,790 persons unemployed in Winnipeg, and 9,599 unemployed in Manitoba at December 31 last. The Hon. Errick Willis stated at a recent meeting that there are 1,200 unemployed carpenters in Winnipeg, and that is typical of the conditions amongst skilled men in this province.
Endeavouring to be completely accurate, may I point out that when I was in Winnipeg recently I spoke with the business agents of certain trade unions. They did not place the figure at 1,200, as did Mr. Willis. Rather they said they believed there were between 600 and 700 unemployed at that time. The letter continues:
Very few plants are in operation more than eight hours per day although capable of handling a wide variety of war requirements if given the opportunity.
After two and a half years of war only a very few plants have been built or appreciably extended to take care of war contracts of any amount. They include the cordite plant near Transcona, MacDonald Bros. Aircraft in Winnipeg and St. James, Dominion Bridge Company, Winnipeg, and the Manitoba rolling mills at Selkirk.
Although large numbers of our skilled workmen have gone east and west to fill positions in war industries in other provinces there still remain thousands on short time or without employment who naturally feel that they should be permitted to make their contribution toward the all-out war effort to which Canada and the empire is pledged. Apparently one of the reasons is that industry is far too concentrated in certain areas in the east while vast areas in the prairies are practically without war plants or war contracts. We are informed that Ontario produces 50 per cent of the manufactured goods made in Canada and Quebec 30 per

cent, that is 80 per cent of Canada's manufacturing production is concentrated in two eastern provinces, leaving only 20 per cent for the other . seven provinces. Manitoba ranks fourth in manufacturing production for Canada but produces only 4 per cent of the total for the dominion. Many communities in the east are so congested with new industries and expanded industries that they are competing for each other's labour and housing has become such a serious problem that War Housing Limited is required to build new homes in those congested districts by the thousands. In Manitoba we have plants which have had very little or no opportunity of manufacturing or subcontracting for war supplies and thousands of skilled workmen whose homes are in the vicinities of these plants should be engaged in production in two or three shifts per 24 hours.
The number of plants in this province operating more than one shift can be counted on one's fingers. Plants in the east are surfeited with war orders which they are months behind in filling. The machine shops of the large paper companies are surfeited with work for war contracts while our machine shops are relatively at a standstill.
Manitoba has well exceeded its proportion of the dominion government's various drives for money, such as the first and second victory loans and war savings certificates.
I read to-day in a Winnipeg paper that in the recent drive they exceeded their quota by 50 per cent. The letter continues:
In addition it has very well, in proportion to its population, supported the three armed services although very badly depleting many farming communities of necessary farm labour in doing so. We feel that the dominion government should see that this provincial area receives a fair share of the war industrial expansion and production, in spending these vast sums of money collected for war purposes.

I do not agree, but they have been good enough to bring down a bill, which of course is very much better than the way in which they handled the summer-fallow last year, by estimate and regulation. After all, however, this leaves power in the hands of the governor in council to legislate, and the principle is objectionable. Having registered that protest I will say no more about it.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: I want to see if I have a clear understanding of section 3. Let us assume that the bill has passed and that the British government now have a credit of one billion dollars in Canada. subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: That is not clear from the legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: I do not like to say yes unless I understand fully what the question is.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: I will try to put it a little more clearly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: The hon. member was pretty clear and I will try to deal with the question. The United Kingdom will continue, I anticipate, to order goods from Canada in the future as they have done in the past, and in some instances it may be that the goods will be bought by the dominion and given without a price being attached to them other than the price which was paid by the dominion government.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: What goods you buy you will buy on request orders from the British government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: Yes. In other instances, though I cannot say that this is what will be done, I expect that the United Kingdom would themselves set the price in agreement with agencies of the dominion government, or the dominion government itself selling Canadian goods-to the United Kingdom, except that no money would be collected for them. Some commodity would be sold at so much a unit and would be charged to the gift. It would be necessary to know the amount of the gift in order to determine when the period of the gift was exhausted.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
For instance, if the British government sends an order to the dominoin government, or through its agencies here, for,
say 4-7 inch guns, one of the items mentioned, when these guns are shipped the price is charged against the credit of one billion dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: Yes, that is right.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: What I am trying to get clear is this. It is a billion dollars of a free gift in goods?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: To help the British government fight the war.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: Is the British government going to set the price on the goods?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: In agreement, I said, with the agency of the dominion government selling the goods.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: They will do what they have been doing up to now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: Exactly.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: The British government will hardly look a gift horse in the mouth and ask what price tag you are putting on this machine or that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: I do not want any such idea to get abroad.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
The
minister's explanation is susceptible of that construction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: I do not expect the dominion government to put two prices on anything.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: I did not suggest that. I said they would not look a gift horse, a free gift, in the mouth, and ask what price tag you were putting on anything in using up the billion dollars. I would not think they would, when they are getting it free, and I did not suggest that there would be two prices. What I think the government ought to do would be to charge against the billion dollar appropriation, the actual, proper cost of the goods in question, delivered to Britain. That is what I hope will be done, and it will be a gift in kind from the Canadian people to Britain. That is what ought to be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: That sounds simpler than it is. There are some articles as to which the cost cannot be ascertained.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
Until
completed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
We anticipate that the transactions will go on just as they have done before. These are to be business transactions,
War Appropriation

the same as if we were seller and they were buyer; otherwise the transaction has no meaning. It makes a big difference with regard to the terminating date of the transaction.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: I agree with that, but that is another matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: It makes a big difference if either party is to be loose about price.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: In the same paragraph reference is made to foodstuffs. In the past year or two there have been agreements between the dominion and British governments in regard to bacon and cheese, and the price that has been paid to the producer in Canada has been considerably above that paid by the British government. Is the same kind of agreement going to enter into this billion dollar transaction?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: That is not correct. The price that has been paid for bacon is the price received by the British government. There was a bonus for a time but there is no longer any bonus. The price for bacon is 100 shillings per hundredweight, obtained from the United Kingdom and paid to the Canadian producer.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: Does that policy apply to wheat as well as to bacon and cheese?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: Does what apply?

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: Is the price paid by Britain that which has been credited to the farmer by the wheat board.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: Absolutely; there is no doubt about that. The wheat board cannot do anything else.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
The wheat board is receiving only the price the farmers get?
Mr. ILSLEY': The wheat board sells the wheat for a certain price, and that price is dealt with in accordance with the provisions of the wheat board act. The wheat board could not do anything else; they could not subtract any part of it.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
There is a belief that the British government has been paying considerably more than the Fort William price of wheat, through the Canadian wheat board, and I am asking the question because of the manner in which another question was put by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox, who inquired about bacon and hogs.
I was wondering whether the same policy carried right through.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
Would the minister say a
few words regarding the general principle of this section as it applies to other allied nations? As I understand it, all the allied nations have undertaken an all-out war effort, to fight the enemy wherever he may be, whether on the shores of England, Australia or America. I think I heard the President of the United States say that the allied nations would pool their resources. If that is the situation, there should be no such thing as inter-allied payments; every nation should turn into the pool the total amount of its production for a common effort. Have there been any discussions in that regard? We are making this gift to Britain, and I think all the allied nations should be turning in their total production for the purpose of defeating the enemy, wherever found, without any question of payment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: I have not sufficient knowledge of those matters to give an answer which would be of value with regard to that.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
Is this likely to be the
beginning of such action on the part of other nations?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
I would not say it is. The principle which the hon. member suggests is perhaps correct; but from our point of view here in Canada we are anxious to keep producing all we possibly can and producing smoothly and without delay in delivery, and one way by which we can ensure ourselves against delays is to keep in a position to get imports from the United States and be able to pay for them. For that reason we have to think about our

War Appropriation
exchange position, our exports to the United States and so on. If we were simply to say we will send the United States anything they want and the United States will send to us anything we want, it might have a prejudicial effect upon deliveries and, indirectly, upon production.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: It would have.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
It is not so simple to get
great pools and governmental agencies to act just whenever and as they should. Those are matters that require a great deal of arranging. Therefore, pending such time as arrangements are made, we have to go on buying and selling, and that is what we are doing. ,

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: Then, if it is not going to be possible to get the nations to contribute their production on a free basis and we are going to have to go on buying a certain proportion of the production of the United States, in view of the fact that the United States must be just as much interested in winning the war as we are they should be anxious that our production be on as effective a basis as possible. We have been told on several occasions that we are reaching or rapidly approaching our maximum production, on account of the shortage of skilled labour. We have at present, I understand, something in the neighbourhood of 32,000 skilled men, miners and mechanics, employed in the goldmining industry. It is not helping the United States war effort in the slightest degree to receive that gold at the present time. They may intend to use it after the war, but it is of no use to their war effort now. If it is necessary for us to pay the United States in gold for the goods we are getting to-day, would it not be possible to hypothecate the production of gold in Canada for so many years after the war and release for the present that labour for use in war industry? That would benefit the United States just as much as ourselves. If, after the war, the United States still want that gold, there would be the possibility of putting all that labour to work in the gold mines after the war and providing employment, but for the time being that labour so necessary for the war effort would be released.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: The question of going out of the gold-mining business in Canada, is a separate one. I do not think it is sufficiently related to this bill to justify us in devoting attention to it now. It is a large question; I would hesitate to make any offhand observations on it, and I would consider it irrelevant to this bill.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: But there is a definite connection. If the United States were turning their goods into the pool as we are, we would not have to turn over gold, and 32,000 men now occupied in mining the gold would be released for war work. Instead of mining it and sending it to be placed in the vaults at Fort Knox, the gold could remain where it is for the time being and that labour be released. Surely the minister is prepared to say why it is considered necessary to mine gold at a time like this. I understand that Russia has stopped the mining of gold for the duration of the war. I am not sure as to that, but I read it in the paper the other day. When we are trying to make an all-out war effort surely we should not carry on a non-essential industry. If the minister is not prepared to make a statement now, I hope that at some time during the session he will be prepared to justify the carrying on of the gold-mining industry.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: Correct.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: If they did, it would not be a business transaction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: They will buy as cheaply as they can, and they will charge against the billion dollars as low a price as they buy the tanks at.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: I do not know just what the course of business is, but I think in the purchase of the tanks the British government gets the Department of Munitions and Supply to produce or buy the tanks, and they get them as cheaply as they can.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: The British government buy as cheaply as they can.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
Yes; I am pretty sure they do, and the Department of Munitions and Supply would get them made as cheaply as possible. They would make a business transaction with the people who produce them. And that will continue. It would make this
War Appropriation

thing ridiculous if we let .the existence of this gift change the business practice that now prevails in the setting of prices and supplying of goods.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: There is a change in law, because heretofore the Minister of Munitions and Supply has been merely the agent of the British government, and now he will be acting for our own government. Certainly there is a legal difference.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: I do not think so. He will continue to be the agent.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: Coming back to the question of foodstuffs, I think the minister will agree that wheat comes under that category, and I think it should be included in this clause. The government have been supplying bacon, cheese and other commodities at agreed prices and, I think, financing the purchases for the British government. We have every reason to believe that in recent months, according to the monthly reports of the minister, wheat has been offered at St. Lawrence ports at considerably over 90 cents a bushel, and no doubt a good deal of it has been sold at that figure. I do not see why the government could not include wheat in this clause, since this really is to be a gift; and the government could finance the British purchases of wheat, as they finance purchases of other foodstuffs.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: The dominion government is not financing the purchase of foodstuffs in any other sense than this, that they are providing the United Kingdom with dollars with which to make their purchases generally in Canada, by buying sterling; that is all.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: Is that not practically the same thing?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: No; it is not financing in one sense at all.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: Then what is the meaning of the word "foodstuffs" in this bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: "Foodstuffs" includes wheat, of course. I thought the hon. gentleman was saying it should include wheat.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: I say it should.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: It does include wheat. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Tripp) brought up that question half an hour ago; he said he wanted to know if it included wheat, and I asked that he should let it go until we came to section 3. There is no necessity to add anything to the word "foodstuffs".

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
Are there any Canadian
National securities, or other Canadian securities, held in Eire? If so, would Eire be

in a position to unload them on Great Britain, so that we in turn would repatriate them under this scheme?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: The British government has not power to take securities away from the residents of Eire and vest them with the British government.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: But suppose the residents of Eire wanted to do it voluntarily. In this bill you designate Great Britain and Northern Ireland. My question is whether those people in Eire holding Canadian securities could unload them on Great Britain, so that under this arrangement we in turn would repatriate them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: That is a question for the British government, I think; but in all probability the British government would not allow the importation of securities from Eire into the United Kingdom, since this would necessitate the export of British capital to Eire in return for the securities. Certainly that would not be permitted by the foreign exchange control authorities in Britain.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: But Eire may have debts owing to Great Britain, and one way of paying those debts would be by Canadian National or other Canadian securities, which we in turn might repatriate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: I am afraid I cannot add anything to what I said. I do not know whether such transactions, even if possible, would be very probable.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
It would be interesting to
know.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: I am not at all sure that they would be prejudicial to us; we would be getting back our securities, anyway. I would have to think about that, to see whether there would be any harm in it.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: It is not the intention, as I understand, for us to interfere with ordinary business practice between the two countries; yet one cannot help but feel that the man who pays the piper usually calls the tune. Is there likely to be any disposition on the part of our government, acting through the Minister of Finance in this case, in authorizing advances or payments for British account, to dictate or suggest to the British government the type of goods or material they shall buy in this country, or is this a straight gift?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
It is a straight gift, without strings. This arrangement is in pursuance of our policy announced a long time ago and concurred in by everyone, to supply the

War Appropriation
United Kingdom with all that the United Kingdom requires for the purpose of carrying on the war. If we interjected a commercial motive into it at this stage, it would be inconsistent with the whole spirit of this transaction and the whole spirit of our policy for some time past.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: It is not a commercial motive; but if we wanted to send tanks instead of aeroplanes, it would not be our intention to dictate to them what they should order from Canada so far as the spending of this billion dollars is concerned? It will be left exactly as it is now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: We certainly would not dictate. On the other hand, of course, there is no doubt that our defence authorities would have views as to what ought to remain in Canada and what should go to the United Kingdom. They at least would be as entitled to those views as the United Kingdom government would be entitled to their views. But I think that is a different matter from what the hon. gentleman has in mind. That is not a case of dictating; it is a case of expressing an opinion as to where rifles should go, or where tanks or aeroplanes should go. If we needed them for the west coast, for example, perhaps we would not send them to Great Britain, or perhaps we would; I do not know. We would have views on that, however, and would not feel obligated to abandon our views.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
Having
regard to the experience of the past year in sending goods to Britain for which we hold certain sterling balances, which are now to be funded, how much of this billion dollars shall we have to send to the United States for materials entering into the manufacture of the goods we are giving to Britain? How much of the money is going to be lost to Canada in the sense that we have to buy from outside this country?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: No estimate of that has been made. If half of this money were spent for foodstuffs, that half would all be spent in Canada; there would be practically nothing imported from the United States in the line of foodstuffs. The same would apply to minerals, mined in Canada, though there might be something there in connection with imported machinery or something like that.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
I am
talking about tanks and aeroplanes, in connection with which we have to import large quantities of goods.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
Yes. We cannot tell. If
we were to take one particular commodity or article, such as tanks or aeroplanes, an estimate could be made.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: Perhaps my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply could tell hon. members what is the United States content of tanks, and what is the Canadian content.

speechtext: Subsection 4 of section 3 deals with the determination of the amount of sterling balances. That is of some importance. subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: And the date of coming into force of the act has some bearing on it also? I presume you want to bring it into force as soon as possible?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: Before the Easter recess.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
I should like to call the attention of the minister to subsection 3 of section 3. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: At the moment I do not see any reason for the difference in wording. I cannot see why you could not say "pay therefor".

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

First you have, "may pay for"; then you have, "pay therefor," and then you have, "may pay for."

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
Subsection 3 of this section reads;
The governor in council may fix a date which shall be deemed to be the termination of the war for the purposes of this section.
In all other legislation this is fixed by the provisions of the War Measures Act. If this subsection should carry * in its present form, you would have an anomalous position. The war might actually be over, not only de jacto but de jure. I wonder whether that is done on purpose? If so, for what purpose? I would suggest that if it is not in contravention of some fixed principle or policy, there should be uniformity.
Mr. ILSLEY; The hon. gentleman is hardly right in saying that in all legislation the date is fixed by the War Measures Act.

It is
