subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: It is left to the governor in council to determine for the purposes of that act, and that may be too late or too early for the purposes of this measure. I went through this matter in negotiating with the provinces. The termination of the agreements with the provinces was designed to be the termination of the war, and at first it was thought we should put into these agreements the date fixed under the War Measures Act as the termination of the war. After much discussion and consideration it was decided not to do that, but to provide for a date which might be different from that date. There is no assurance that that date will coincide with the termination of hostilities. In fact, it does not have any relation to the termination of hostilities. If one puts in, "the termination of hostilities," that might prove to be a controversial date. It might be urged by one party to the agreement that hostilities have ended, and by others that some hostilities are still in progress. Therefore, there has to be power vested in some body to make a decision in the matter and fix a date. For our purposes we think this is the way to do it, to leave it to the governor in council to fix a date for the termination of the war for the purposes of the act.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
That is a convenient thing to do. I have sent out for a copy of the War Measures Act because I have not the text in front of me. I should like to point out to the minister that probably the reason is that when the war ceases under the War Measures Act, the changes in the British North America Act brought about by the War Measures Act, including the control of everything under which we are being regimented, stop immediately. The ordinary principles of the Canadian constitution then become operative, and price ceilings and all the rest of it go by the board. There is no doubt about that, and that may be the reason for this. I do not say it is, but I am pointing that out. These gentlemen who are talking about planned economy after the war had better put on their thinking caps and read a few cases on the constitution. They will then ascertain that after the war is over, there will be no more wartime prices and trade board; there will be no more controllers bobbing up and setting a ceiling on maple syrup to the habitants in the province of Quebec; there will be no more interference with the principles of

War Appropriation
the British North America Act with respect to property and civil rights; there will be no more freezing of wages by order in council.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
I hope the hon. member is
right, but I am doubtful.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
I am
telling you, and I can give you some cases which you can read for yourself. If we are going to have this planned economy, which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) talks about, in the post-war days we shall have to have a new constitution in this country. I should like to see him get it, having regard to the fact that you would have to persuade not only this parliament-I am also talking for the benefit of the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) who, I see is taking down a few notes-but the nine provincial legislatures. I think you will find that is true, because they will not change the British North America Act, over there, on the other side, without the consent of the provinces. They will not take away from the provinces the powers conferred upon them by imperial acts of parliament with respect to property and civil rights, without the consent of the provinces. I will tell you that Quebec will fight it to the limit-and they will be right-because we would have centralized in the central government of Canada too much power. I would be content to see the centralization of currency, credit control and matters of that kind. But with respect to property and civil rights the subject is far safer under the present system than he would be with centralized control. I believe the people of Quebec will agree with me that they will be much safer under the present system than under one of centralized control.
This is a piece of free legal advice I am giving. It will not cost my hon. friends anything. And, if they want me to, I shall cite the cases to back up my opinion.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: If it does not cost anything, then I imagine from a lawyer's point of view it is not worth much.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: It cost me a lot to learn.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: I am not going to argue about the constitution to-night. Constitutions are made for men, not men for constitutions. When the people of this country decide; when all the provinces and the dominion decide that economic and social conditions make the amendment of the constitution necessary, the Dominion of Canada is going to amend her own constitution. Make no mistake about that. That will be done, when the time comes and it is found to be necessary.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: But with the consent of the provinces.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
It will be done when it is necessary. Let me say this, that while some people think there is a safeguard in the fact that we are unable to amend our own constitution, and that it has to be amended by the imperial parliament, I am willing to wager that any request which came from Canada by way of a clear majority vote now would be approved by the imperial parliament almost without discussion. They would not wish to interfere with the expressed will of a majority of the Canadian people. That, in my opinion, is the situation as it stands to-day.
I had not intended to say that, but the leader of the opposition provoked me to it. What I did rise to say is that we are dealing with section 4 of the bill, and it appears that under that section a loan of $700,000,000 is to be made to Great Britain, without interest, for the duration of the war. I do not think anyone is going to disapprove the making of the loan under circumstances as they are to-day. But I am going to suggest that in making the loan the whole problem of the repatriation of the remaining securities now outstanding in Great Britain should be gone into, and that they might be regarded as tantamount to collateral against this loan to be dealt with, if you like, at the termination of the war.
I have been thinking a great deal about what was said the other day by the Minister of Finance with respect to the gift, the reasons for it, and the loan. I disagree entirely with the point of view that we should not contemplate repatriation of the remaining securities held in Great Britain, so that we might have them in our own dominion and, as I should like to see them, in the hands of the government, in order that we might have a greater control of industry-and particularly certain monopolistic industries-than we have to-day.
We shall need this when the war is over, if we are going to rehabilitate this country. I believe it would be to the advantage of the people of this country if in the making of such loans we could contemplate in the future that we could recover from any overseas investors the securities they now hold upon industries, and other enterprise, in Canada.
For example, we have the railways problem. I am not in favour of any unification or amalgamation such as has been suggested or of the handing over of our government road to any form of private management. But I do believe that probably the war will thrust upon us, during its progress, a greater measure of control over our whole transportation system.
War Appropriation

I should like to see bus and truck services used to feed the railways, instead of to compete with them. I believe that would save both tires and gasoline, and after the war it would assist us in developing a real transportation system.
As I said the other afternoon there are in Great Britain, among other securities, some 8596,600,000, par value, of Canadian Pacific Railway stock and debentures. I can see no reason at all why these stocks and bonds should not at least be regarded as collateral against this loan of $700,000,000. I do not subscribe to the point of view that we should endeavour to remain a debtor nation to Great Britain simply because some believe that that would enable us to export goods there in payment of the interest and dividends on our debt beyond the seas. To my mind, carried to its logical conclusion, such an argument implies that the man who owes the most should be the best off, because he would have to pay the most to a creditor, and that would mean that he would have to hand over more and more of the fruits of his labour.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: May I ask a question? Mr. COLDWELL: Yes.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: How would the hon. member take over the several millions of dollars worth of Canadian Pacific Railway securities? They belong to private investors.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: They belong to private investors, my hon. friend says. But the British government to-day is causing or compelling British investors to hand securities held in Great Britain over to the government when called upon to do so. We are going to repatriate another block of Canadian National bonds which were held by private individuals in Great Britain.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: We guaranteed them.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
It does not matter whether we guaranteed them or not. They are in the hands of private investors. They have securities and we have given a guarantee. But that does not place them in any other category, so far as the ownership of the bonds or stock goes in Great Britain; they are or have been privately owned. Everyone holding an overseas security must register it and, if called upon by the government, he must surrender it to the government. That is the well-defined plan or policy Britain has adopted, and Canadian Pacific Railway stocks are no exception.
Naturally the British government will pay the British investor in sterling funds-but that is being done in all cases. Canadian Pacific Railway stock is in no different position. It 
is up to the British government to make their own arrangements with their own people. It is up to us to make the best arrangements we can for the Canadian people. I am pointing out that with relation to stocks and bonds of this description-we will say securities of International Nickel, and some of the other larger corporations in this country-we are derelict in our duty if, in addition to making a gift of a billion dollars outright, which we have all supported, we make a loan and leave over there securities which might be repatriated to this country eventually, and which would relieve us of the payment of interest and dividends to any investors beyond the seas.
Of course, if these securities are resold in Canada, there may be some slight advantage. If they are resold to investors, we will say, in the United States, then there is little or no advantage in that regard, because you would just be changing one set of creditors in one country for another set of creditors in another country. But I want to emphasize that from my point of view-and I believe I am expressing the point of view of many people in this dominion-in the making of this loan we should proceed-as we are told trades in goods between Great Britain and this country are made-on sound business principles.
I suppose that the British purchaser insists that the goods he buys from Canada shall be bought at prices comparable with those of goods of the same type which he can get elsewhere. I think wTe should view the loan- not the gift; I make the distinction very clearly'-from exactly the same business point of view, and we should as far as possible protect our own country and its future by asking at least that these securities be placed as collateral against this loan, so that, when we come to determine what shall be done at the termination of the war, we may, if it seems advantageous on both sides to do it, be in a position to repatriate bonds and stocks of Canadian corporations for the benefit of this country. I believe that is the businesslike point of view to take. I know that if there is one group in the world who-quite properly-enter into transactions on a businesslike basis, it is the British business man. I remember Mr. Bennett, when he was leader of the opposition in this house, talking about the imperial conference in 1932 and explaining that the British did not allow sentiment to interfere with their business transactions, even when negotiating empire trade agreements; and we, I think, having made a gift, should see to it, in making the loan, that it is made on a sound and proper business basis to protect this country in the days which follow the war.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: Perhaps I am wrong, but the billion dollars has to come from somewhere ; whether it comes from taxation, or from debt incurred which will eventually mean taxation, I do not know; but it does figure out at about $100 per capita on all the people of Canada, that they will be called upon to pay either now, next year or a thousand years from now. That is the position. If a proportion of this is going to be raised by way of loan, particularly if any part comes from the Bank of Canada, could that not be lent to the government without interest? That, I believe, is a fair question, and I think considerable progress would be made in the fiscal policy of the country if something like that were brought about.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
The only way to get a loan without interest is by compulsion, and the whole issue of compulsory loans would have to be faced. Both sides of that question have been argued in other sessions. I have not brought myself to the place where I feel it would be wise to propose a system of compulsory loans in Canada. I do not think anything would be gained by going into that issue now.
But the point I should like to make clear is that the making of a gift to Britain instead of lending the money to Britain does not impose any further obligation on the Canadian people. The gift feature of it does not cost us $100 a head; it is the making of the equipment, the producing and forwarding of the goods that takes so much of the energies and resources of the Canadian people. Whether we give it or sell it or lend it to Great Britain, the effect on the Canadian people is exactly the same.
The other question, whether as part of our general policy we should obtain money by compulsory loans instead of voluntary loans, is an issue which is in no way related to this. This does not make the case any stronger or any weaker for compulsory loans versus voluntary loans. There would be no advantage as far as I can see in charging interest to Great Britain for the $700 million, because it would render their requirements for Canadian dollars that much greater and so exhaust the billion dollar gift that much sooner. And since it will probably be exhausted in the early part of 1943 anyway, it would to a certain extent affect the transaction if we were to do it. I do not think there really would be any advantage to us in shortening that period somewhat by charging interest on this money, which is the only effect it would have.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
A moment ago the question was raised as to the advisability of raising what money must be borrowed through the Bank of Canada, interest free, not so much as a forced loan but as a cooperative loan which the Bank of Canada would make to the dominion because it is the Bank of Canada and because it is the dominion, and because the two of them are serving the Canadian people. The minister did not make any definite pronouncement on the subject. It is a confused question, and one about which there is great diversity of opinion. I just wish to tell the minister now that when the two billion dollar war appropriation bill comes before the house we shall ask him for an explanation why it would not be advisable to raise that money in that way. We are refraining from discussing the matter on this bill because we wish to help the minister get this bill through, in order that some business may be cleared up before the Easter recess. But we do believe it is possible to obtain this money at very low interest rates, and possibly without interest at all, and we think it will be impossible for the minister to show us to the contrary.
There is one more thing it might be well for me to say here. I laid down in my speech on Friday what I think is a safe assumption, that this one billion dollar gift to Britain is going to mean probably $500,000,000 collected from the people of Canada in taxes and $500,000,000 to be borrowed by the government from either the people, the banks or other institutions, and upon which there will be at least 2 per cent interest practically in perpetuity. This will mean the virtual saddling of the Canadian people for ages, at least for generations, with $10,000,000 annually in interest charges. I think I am safe in making this assumption. This is all I have to say at the present time.

speechtext:
That, of course, depends on the government. I suggest that if the government does not wish to have all the-ministers here at one time, it should make-arrangements to have one of them here at a time and have his department discussed.. Then, when that department has been completed, we could go on to another minister. That might have been done last year, and if it had, our discussions would have been far more easily followed, and far more businesslike.
The resolution under debate to-night might be described as a declaration to the effect that it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide an additional $135,000,000 for Canada's war effort during the current year which, as hon. members know, ends in eight days, on March 31, 1942. As the minister has just explained, that will make a total expenditure for war purposes during the-current year of about $1,435,000,000. For the-year 1942-43 war expenditures are to be over $2,200,000,000, if I understood the minister correctly when he spoke the other night. That is an increase for -the coming fiscal year of approximately 50 per cent. In addition there is a billion dollars for aid to Great Britain.
Those are huge sums, but there will be little complaint from the people of Canada. Provided the money is fairly spent and that it is not wasted, they will approve the voting of these sums. To understand the reason for their approval one need only compare the present position with the position last.
War Appropriation

year. In the twelve months which have intervened the war has become a world war. Russia has come in as an ally of the British nations. Japan has gone in with Germany and Italy. The United States, our great neighbour, has come in with us. So that now it is a case of the united nations against the axis powers, in a struggle to the death. That was well described by General McNaughton when he used these words in Montreal on February 6:
This is a war in which the whole forces of science have been fixed by the enemy on one purpose alone, and that is our death.
"Our death"-that is the objective of the axis powers. Canadians know these facts and, as I have said, they will approve the raising of these moneys. They also know that beyond our eastern shores the British nations are still the bulwark against a nazi move to the west, and that they are preparing to strike out. They know that over there, in Great Britain, is our own Canadian army ready to go into action at a moment's notice.
On the other side beyond our western shores, our people know that Singapore is now in the hands of the enemy. Java is gone, and we hear Japan threatening our sister dominion of Australia. On March 11 the Japanese premier is reported to have used these words:
The best and only way for Australia to take was shown by Premier Hideki Tojo when he declared that if the Australian people continued their present attitude "we will show no mercy in crushing them."
Australia is preparing desperately, and at the same time she is warning other nations, including Canada. She is giving a warning, as indicated in these words spoken by the Prime Minister of Australia about ten days ago:
But I give you this warning. Australia is the last bastion between the west coast of America and the Japanese. If Australia goes, the Americas are wide open. It is said that the Japanese will by-pass Australia, and that they can be met and routed in India. I say to you that the saving of Australia is the saving of America's west coast. If you believe anything to the contrary, then you delude yourselves.
May I repeat those words: "If you believe .anything to the contrary, then you delude yourselves."
At this point I urge upon the ministry that they send at least a token force to Australia. Canada is a Pacific nation, a nation on the Pacific. It may be that Canada's best defence on the Pacific will be by fighting in Australia. For that reason alone-for that selfish reason alone, if for no

other-we should have troops standing beside the Australian troops. Furthermore we are a sister nation in the British commonwealth. We fought beside the Australians in the last war, and we have a brotherly feeling towards them in this one. Their young airmen have come here to take training. Surely Canada should not hang back. We should send at least a token force to Australia at the earliest possible moment.
Further than that, Australia is asking that a Pacific council be set up with headquarters in Washington; and the minister who came from Australia the other day suggested that Canada should have a member on that council. We have brought forward that suggestion in the house on two or three occasions, but as yet the ministry have not seen fit to act.
I urge upon them that they endorse the plea of Australia for the setting up of a Pacific council in Washington, and that Canada ask for representation on that council.
I believe everyone here will agree that the Canadian people see this nation menaced directly at its gates on either ocean. They know and we know that 1942 is the critical year. There is yet no certainty that Canada will survive. I thought the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) put it very clearly when, in his radio address eleven or twelve days ago, he said:
The present is the crucial year. Germany and Japan are staking everything on 1942.
He went on to say-and the house should mark every word of this utterance:
The survival of every nation is at stake. Now, more than at any other time, the maximum force of the united nations must be brought into action.
No, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian people do not object to the spending of two billion dollars in the next twelve months on the war effort. But-and there is a "but"-it is not enough for the ministry and for this parliament to raise and spend money. The Canadian people are asking-they are demanding, and quite properly so-that this ministry, and this parliament-it is not a matter for the ministry alone-should lead them boldly in waging war. We in the House of Commons are the elected representatives of the people. We cannot evade this responsibility, a responsibility so great and so challenging, because of the nation's peril, that it should be an inspiration to every hon. member.
What can we do to lead the Canadian people in waging war? First of all, I think, comes the attitude of mind. It always seems to me that the mental approach to these questions is of the utmost importance, and I suggest that we in this parliament can help, by the

War Appropriation
attitude we have in our minds, by realizing clearly and remembering constantly, not only for an hour now and an hour again, but constantly, that practically every day some young Canadian airman dies to help keep this nation free-that is a thing to be remembered by the members of this house-by realizing that to-day, not next month or next year, the Canadian army overseas may be locked in a death struggle with the nazis in Great Britain or be in the van of an invasion of the continent; by realizing that to-day, not next month, cities, towns and villages of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, and the St. Lawrence district of Quebec, may be bombed from the air or bombarded from the sea; that to-day or to-morrow Japanese invaders may be on Canada's Pacific coast, in my own province of British Columbia, tying up Canadian prisoners of war and bayoneting them to death, and raping and murdering our women as they did in Hong Kong.
We must realize these things ourselves and convince our people that they, too, must face these ugly facts. Mr. Speaker, the ministry and parliament and the Canadian people must plan and act accordingly. There are many things which can and must be done. Every ounce of our national strength must be directed to waging war. That is not so now, and I propose to give several examples.
First, there has been a great increase in the production and sale of non-war goods. A short time ago very interesting articles appeared under the hand of Grant Dexter, one of the leading members of the press gallery, in which he set out a list of non-war articles and showed how the amount spent on them increased from 1939 to 1941. I propose to give several of his figures in round numbers:

There has been a great increase in production of non-war articles which he sums up in these words:
Thus we have stepped up the production of musical instruments, furniture, silk stockings, clothing, tobacco, beverages, glassware and heating appliances.
Another distressing aspect of this condition is that it has made a great increase in the number of people producing non-war articles, as he says:
We have devoted man-power to these purposes. . . . Three hundred and thirty-nine thousand pairs of hands have gone to work since the war began at jobs which have small war significance.	*
I believe every hon. member knows that these things are going on in his or her constituency. It is a situation which should be checked at once. Action should be taken to direct much of this portion of our national strength to waging war. That would mean a release for war purposes of man and woman power, and of materials, money, and the equipment for manufacturing goods.
Donald Gordon, chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, said much the same thing when he spoke in Montreal late last week. He is quoted in the press as having said:
We must be prepared to give up all our choices and preferences and accustom ourselves to a standard of living based on bare essentials, for only by so doing can we divert to war the maximum of our productive effort which is the prime requirement for total war.
But direction from the ministry is necessary, and it is not being given at this time. The Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power), speaking in Montreal on December 13, shortly after Japan struck, used these words:
These powers-
Referring to the powers given to the government under the National Resources Mobilization Act.
-we propose to use in the emergency which confronts us and in an endeavour to see to it that every man and woman in this country carries on the work which will be of the greatest possible benefit to the state as a whole.
That was nearly four months ago, and it is about time that the government took the advice of the minister and got busy on the programme which he outlined at that time. If he had been in charge of carrying out the programme, something would have been done long since.
It would help if the ministry would ask those Canadians who are serving on the home front to buy on the basis of "How little do I need; what can I do without?" rather than on the present basis, which seems to be, "How much can I get and how long can I get this or that?" If the Canadian people are shown that every dollar spent on supplies not absolutely necessary may mean less war material produced or fewer men in the fighting forces, they will respond. The government from the start of the war have made the mistake of not asking the Canadian people for enough, not asking them to do as much as the people have been and are prepared to do.
War Appropriation

That brings me to the fighting forces-manpower-and I am glad to see the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) in his seat. The position in respect of man-power is much the same. We are not using our available man-power. Although Japan struck over three months ago and Canada's position became infinitely more dangerous, the defence department has gone placidly on calling on the Department of National War Services for about the same number of men-no hurry apparently, no urgency, plenty of time to get men and give them training. Now we find this situation. I quote from a press dispatch by Mr. Carnegie of the Canadian Press on March 14:
The supply of man-power to keep up the flow of compulsory service recruits to the training centres at the rate of 5,000 a month has *diminished to such an extent that the age limit shortly will be advanced probably to 30 years, a government authority said to-day.
It is my understanding that no men are being called above the age of twenty-six. If that is not correct, I ask the minister to correct me. Meanwhile the Australians have made provision to call men for military service up to the age of sixty. Our ministry apparently expect that men from nineteen to thirty-five are to do the fighting in the active army. If that is so-and I do not think it will be denied

those men should be given training at once; they should be called up without further delay and given a chance to get proper training, which in the long run may mean the saving of the lives of many of them, and will certainly mean a stronger and more efficient fighting force. Instead of that, we are to have another survey or registration of some kind, which again will take weeks.
Something should be done now about the size of our active army. It should be increased. On February 10, speaking in this house, the Minister of National Defence said, as reported at page 451 of Hansard:
It should be remembered that apart from the fourth division and the brigade groups of the sixth division, we have in Canada over 110.000 active service personnel in training centres and elsewhere.
Since then, I believe about 10,000 have enlisted, but-and here again there is a "but"- many, many thousands of these men are pinned down; they are engaged in some particular army work so that they cannot be moved about. For example there are men on the training centre staffs and men on the district depot staffs and on headquarters staffs, and many of the men in the veterans' guard, men in detachments on the home war establishments and attached to the air force, men in permanent hospitals, and thousands of coast defence troops. There are many more thousands who are reinforcements for overseas,
IMr. Green.]
with the result that there is a comparatively small number to form mobile forces in Canada. We should have larger mobile forces in Canada; for example, on the Pacific coast at the present time we should have a striking force. In the first place, that would be the best way to defend our coast, by building up a force that could be rushed from one part of the coast to another. It should not be a matter of a few hundred men here and there but a proper striking force. The time will come, I hope, when we shall be able to send a striking force out over the Pacific, and in the meantime men could be trained in British Columbia for that purpose.
The province of British Columbia should be treated as a war front, just as Great Britain is treated as a war front. I cannot understand, for example, why the rule which calls for younger men in command of the different units should not apply in British Columbia just as it applies in Great Britain. The forces on the Pacific coast under present conditions should be handled as though they were on a war front, which is actually the case.
Then we should do something now about our reserve force. It should be increased. This little government publication called "Canada at War", which comes out every month, says at page 8 of the supplement of February 1:
At home, a special reorganization and regrouping is being planned for the reserve army, which consists of about 140,000 men.
Over one-third of these men, I believe, are recruits who were called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act for 30-day training. They are carried as supernumerary to establishment, which means that they are merely names on the walls of the different armouries across Canada. No doubt many of them have since enlisted in the fighting forces, and yet these men are shown as a portion of the Canadian reserve army. The result is that the Canadian people think they have
140,000	men in the reserve army, while actually they have very many under that number. Provision should be made so that the men who come within this classification can actually train with the other men in the reserve forces. If necessary, if the ministry cannot recruit the reserve army in any other way, let them call up men over thirty-five for the purpose.
They must give this reserve army some equipment. In my own province of British Columbia there has now been a brigade formed in the reserve army; the men who are joining up are joining up to fight, to be in a position to defend their homes, and if enthusiasm is to be maintained and the brigade is to become efficient, they must be given proper equip-

War Appropriation
ment. It must not be a ease of sending them a field gun or two, a mortar or two, or a small amount of equipment with which they can merely train; they must have weapons with which to fight.
Then I suggest the time has come when we must organize a home guard in Canada. That is particularly true on our war front on the west coast and, I believe, also on the east coast. Certainly on the Pacific coast every able-bodied man should be in the home guard or in air raid precaution work or preparing in some way to take his part should there be an invasion of that coast. At the present time the government has extended the reserve army to some extent by forming small companies in a few centres on the Pacific coast. But it should go much further. Every ablebodied man in British Columbia should be trained and put in some position where he can take his part should the province be invaded.
Another thing that should be done at once or very shortly is that we should produce more equipment. The troops on duty in Canada are not fully equipped-I do not think the minister will deny that. These troops should be equipped, for example, with planes and tanks. The government boasts a great deal about shipping military equipment all over the world; every week some press dispatch is given out to tell of Canada shipping military equipment to all parts of the world. I do not quarrel with that, but the position is just this serious, that Canada must go one step further and produce enough equipment to arm her own troops at home, who may be called upon to defend this nation.
Finally, the ministry should make plans to help the Canadian people meet any eventuality. For example, have plans been made for the evacuation of women and children from either coast in the event of attack? If not, such plans should be made now while we have a chance to do it without great haste, and the leaders in the different communities should know those plans so that there will not be great confusion if trouble comes.
Another question is, is Canada to adopt a scorched-earth policy or is she not? That decision should not be left until the enemy is at our gates. We find Australia on March 10 putting through regulations which are described as follows:
The government is empowered to order the civil evacuation of any area threatened by invasion and in cases where property and live stock cannot be removed their destruction may be ordered.
The regulations also provide for demolition of buildings, public works, airports, railways, mines and reservoirs in such emergencies.
The ministers may smile; some may think this is funny. But may I impress upon them with all the power at my command that things like this should be planned now; there is no better way of instilling confidence in the Canadian people than to have plans prepared and thoroughly understood to meet eventualities of this type.
Each thing I have advocated could be and, I believe, should be done now. There has been too much delay. I can understand that the ministers are overburdened with work, under pressure every day and for long hours, with all kinds of things to do, but there has been much delay and there should be no more. We should get right down to business and start doing these things of the nature I have outlined. Delay is one of the greatest menaces to Canadian survival. I ask the ministry to tell us-and tell us before the Easter adjournment, not on April 20-and through this house tell the Canadian people what they propose to do about these things I have mentioned and other things of the same kind. I urge them and urge every member of this house to give this nation at once far more aggressive leadership in waging war.
